candidates.title: Boundary-Aware Policy Learning for Agent-Orchestrated Robot Manipulation
candidates.introExcerpt: Agent-orchestrated robot systems combine the general reasoning capability of multimodal agents with the precise physical control of learned visuomotor policies. Yet such systems often fail at the moment of handoff: a policy is reliable only from a limited set of start states, while the agent may invoke it outside this region. We call this region the policy's handoff boundary. Existing whole-task policies typically have handoff boundaries that are narrow and difficult for an agent to characterize, making reliable coordination challenging. We propose Boundary-Aware Policy Learning, which explicitly shapes and then expands the handoff boundary of a visuomotor policy. First, Boundary-Explicit Training fine-tunes the policy on contact segments with diverse start poses, yielding a wide and well-defined boundary that can be communicated to the agent through a simple handoff protocol. Second, Boundary-Expanding Self-Improvement retrains the policy on curated successful system rollouts, extending the boundary toward earlier stages of each task and allowing the agent to hand over sooner with fewer language-model calls. Across RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo, our system outperforms the strongest baseline by over 26 percentage points, reaching 98.4% success in randomized RoboTwin 2.0 scenes, while further reducing its API cost and execution time by 41.3% and 37.5%, respectively. These results suggest that the key to robust agent-policy orchestration lies not only in improving either component individually, but also in explicitly shaping the boundary between them.

candidates.title: Reading, Not Adapting: Unlocking Frozen Visual Knowledge for AI-Generated Image Detection
candidates.introExcerpt: Generalization to unseen image generators has driven efforts to adapt pretrained visual representations for detection. Yet recent findings show that vision foundation models already encode transferable detection knowledge, while further adaptation can impair generalization. This motivates a shift from backbone adaptation to knowledge readout. Conventional linear probing offers a direct way to read this knowledge but is limited to final-layer RGB features. Multi-cue detectors broaden the evidence base, but their designs introduce other tradeoffs: adaptation may compromise pretrained transferability, heterogeneous encoders complicate feature integration, and late fusion precludes intermediate cross-view interaction. To overcome these limitations, we propose ReMoT, a Mixture-of-Transformers-inspired framework that reads complementary knowledge from spatially aligned RGB and wavelet views within a fully frozen visual foundation. ReMoT employs staged joint attention to enable controlled local and global cross-view interaction, while learnable fusion queries progressively read complementary evidence across Transformer depth without writeback. ReMoT achieves 91.2% average accuracy across eight benchmark groups with 3,074 trainable parameters, attaining the highest overall average among the evaluated methods. These results support structured knowledge readout as a promising alternative to backbone adaptation. Code is available at https://github.com/yunncheng/ReMoT.

candidates.title: OS-Omni: Benchmarking Generalist Computer-Using Agents on Long-Horizon Workflows Across Platforms
candidates.introExcerpt: Computer-using agents are increasingly expected to complete realistic user goals rather than isolated GUI actions. However, existing benchmarks typically isolate web, mobile, or desktop environments, leaving it unclear whether a single generalist agent can execute long-horizon workflows that span multiple operating systems and persistent application states. We introduce OS-Omni, a live cross-platform benchmark and execution environment for evaluating computer-using agents across Windows, Ubuntu, macOS, iOS, Android, and Web environments. OS-Omni is released in versioned waves of 300 tasks each; this paper focuses on the first release, v1, which contains 48 tasks per platform and 12 cross-platform workflows that pair a desktop with an Android phone. OS-Omni provides reproducible initialization, platform-specific adapters, trajectory logging, and executable final-state evaluators, and includes controlled service-backed applications for workflows involving account, cart, budget, calendar, message, and other persistent state. Human studies show that OS-Omni tasks require 67.54 interaction steps, substantially exceeding OSWorld references of 15.0 steps. On v1, the strongest evaluated agent, Claude Opus 5.5, reaches 68.5% average success, trailing the 77.3% human reference by 8.8 points; the gap is uneven across platforms, with frontier models exceeding humans on Linux but trailing them by more than 25 points on iOS and macOS. These results indicate that current agents remain far from platform-robust, long-horizon computer use, especially when success requires sustained state tracking and durable final-state changes.

candidates.title: DRBench Pro: A Knowledge-Centric Benchmark for Professional Deep Research Agents
candidates.introExcerpt: Deep research agents gather information from multiple sources and synthesize it into reports on complex, open-ended questions. Existing benchmarks assess report quality along several dimensions, but lack a dedicated knowledge-centric evaluation of which research directions a report covers and how deeply it explores them. We introduce DRBench Pro, a benchmark that makes structured knowledge coverage the primary evaluation target. Our automated pipeline builds local knowledge trees from Wikipedia and uses sampled subgraphs to generate research queries and evidence-grounded rubrics. Each rubric corresponds to a relation in the tree, preserving the structure of the knowledge being evaluated. Agents receive only the research query. This structure allows us to measure breadth across major research directions and depth along related knowledge chains, with their geometric mean giving overall coverage. The benchmark includes 144 cases across 24 domains and 44,102 rubrics. Evaluating 16 deep research agents reveals different strengths in breadth and depth, with the best-performing agent reaching 57.04% overall coverage. Rubric judgments agree closely with human annotations, and agent rankings remain stable across the tested metric configurations.

candidates.title: Decision-Native Multimodal Clinical Modeling via Anatomical Grounding and Confidence Calibration
candidates.introExcerpt: Structured clinical decisions from volumetric computed tomography (CT) require anatomically grounded predictions and calibrated confidence estimates. However, existing 3D medical multimodal models often suffer from uncalibrated autoregressive decoding and shortcut reliance on irrelevant anatomical regions. We introduce Radev, a decision-native multimodal model that integrates anatomy-guided visual compression, direct candidate prediction, and counterfactual confidence supervision. To bridge global context with fine-grained slice details, a frozen 3D encoder extracts reusable organ-level features, which are dynamically selected by the query to attend to 2D slice features within predicted anatomical bounds. The resulting compact visual tokens enable the language backbone to estimate candidate probabilities in a single forward pass without autoregressive decoding. We further propose Counterfactual-Calibrated Training (CCT) to compare predictions under intact and intervened organ representations. CCT encourages confidence to decrease when removing target-organ evidence degrades decision quality, while penalizing excessive confidence drops under unrelated-organ removal. To facilitate rigorous evaluation, we construct CT-Verdict, a comprehensive benchmark spanning binary finding presence, multiple-choice questions, and ordinal severity assessment across both in-distribution and external cohorts. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Radev significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both decision accuracy and confidence calibration, while generalizing robustly under distribution shifts. Project page at https://juntaojianggavin.github.io/projects/Radev/

candidates.title: Islamic Social Financial Instruments and Sustainable Community Development: Evidence Synthesis on Community Resilience
candidates.venue: Journal of Islamic Monetary Economics and Finance
candidates.introExcerpt: This study investigates how Islamic Social Finance (ISF)—through zakat, waqf, and sadaqah—supports sustainable community development by strengthening economic, social, institutional, psychological, and environmental resilience. Using a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review and bibliometric analysis of 93 studies published between 2010 and 2025, the paper synthesizes fragmented scholarship to identify the mechanisms through which ISF enhances resilience. Findings show that zakat provides short-term stabilization and crisis relief, waqf enables long-term asset creation and public-goods provision, and sadaqah delivers flexible emergency support. Integrated ZISWAF models, particularly those inspired by Ascarya, emerge as the most effective structure for maximizing development outcomes when supported by strong governance, institutional coordination, and digital innovation. The study contributes (i) a consolidated evidence highlighting thematic fragmentation in ISF research; (ii) an integrated conceptual map linking ISF to resilience theory and the SDGs; and (iii) a multidimensional framework explaining how ISF instruments jointly foster community resilience. Policy recommendations include strengthening governance and regulatory coherence, accelerating digital transformation, adopting integrated ZISWAF delivery models, and expanding ISF applications in environmental sustainability and climate resilience.

candidates.title: Determinants of Financial Inclusion in the OIC and OECD Countries: Are They Different?
candidates.venue: Journal of Islamic Monetary Economics and Finance
candidates.institution: International Centre for Education in Islamic Finance
candidates.introExcerpt: Financial inclusion is a pivotal policy tool to help integrate the underprivilege segments of society into the formal financial system. The issue is particularly important within predominantly Muslim nations, where poverty and inequality remain persistent challenges, and where a significant proportion of the populace remains excluded from financial services. This seems to be paradoxical, especially given the substantial expansion of Islamic finance over the previous decade. Therefore, this research aims to investigate the factors that determine financial inclusion within Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) member states. To put our findings into perspective, we compare our analysis with Organisation of Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) countries. We used a least squares dummy variable (LSDV) estimator across 35 OIC and OECD countries over the period 2005 to 2021. It was found that in OIC countries income per capita, tertiary education attainment, institutional quality, internet accessibility, population and age dependency have an influence on financial inclusion. Unlike OECD ones, OIC countries need to make significant investment in digital infrastructures, youth and female empowerment, and boosting income levels. Lessons are also drawn for Islamic banking in these countries.

candidates.title: Examining the Impact of Waqf Literacy on Waqf Behaviour
candidates.venue: Journal of Islamic Monetary Economics and Finance
candidates.introExcerpt: This paper investigates the impact of waqf literacy on waqf donation of Muslims in Indonesia. It applies the Partial Least Square - Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to data from 642 respondents. Using the Theory of Planned Behaviour (TPB) framework extended to past behaviour as an additional component, we find that waqf literacy positively impacts attitude, social norms, perceived behavioural control (PBC), and past behaviour. In addition, it has an indirect influence on waqf intention through those four TPB components. Moreover, the non-linearity test finds the quadratic effect of waqf literacy on most TPB components. This finding shows significant contribution of Waqf literacy on Muslims’ waqf donation indirectly through the Theory of Planned Behaviour. As a result, all waqf stakeholders should pay more attention toward waqf literacy in order to boost waqf collection.

candidates.title: Trends and Determinants of Sustainability Sukuk Issuance: Evidence from Global Markets
candidates.venue: Journal of Islamic Monetary Economics and Finance
candidates.introExcerpt: Despite the growing prominence of sustainability sukuk in the global realm of sustainable finance, little is known about the dynamics of their issuance. This study is the first to document the evolution of sustainability sukuk issuance and explore the determinants of its size. Using a cross-country sukuk dataset comprising 11,944 issuances between 2012 (i.e., the year when the first sustainability sukuk was issued) to 2022, it highlights that sustainability sukuk remains a minuscule fraction of overall sukuk markets, and its rapid growth during the last recent years is mostly concentrated in Islamic finance-oriented countries like Indonesia, Malaysia, and Saudi Arabia, while other developing Muslim-majority nations show limited participation. Examining determinants, we find that a higher security quality, a more extended debt structure, and major international currency denominations (e.g., USD and Euro) positively influence the size of the sustainability sukuk issue. Additionally, we uncover two unique drivers of sustainability sukuk issuance. The first is second party opinion, where its increased costs reduce issue size. The second is the underlying equity-based Islamic contracts, which encourage larger issuances compared to sale-based contracts. Our results also indicate that issuances by government entities and financial institutions, and those raised for social purposes rather than green projects, tend to be larger. Lastly, we find that a higher level of economic development and greater reliance on international trade in the issuing country may lead to a larger issue size. This paper concludes by calling for policies and incentives to encourage future sustainability sukuk issuance. ACKNOWLEDGMENT The author acknowledges the support of the Securities Commission Malaysia in awarding the fellowship at the Oxford Centre for Islamic Studies, during which this paper was completed.

candidates.title: From Clicks to Credit: AI-Measured Halal Product Awareness and Halal Financing Depth across OIC Countries
candidates.venue: Journal of Islamic Monetary Economics and Finance
candidates.introExcerpt: This study investigates the relationship between consumer-driven halal product awareness and the depth of Islamic financing across selected Organisation of Islamic Cooperation (OIC) countries. Using panel data from 16 OIC member countries over the period 2014–2023, the study examines whether AI-derived halal awareness, proxied by online search intensity, drives total Islamic financing volume and its key components, namely Mudarabah, Murabaha, Musharakah, and Ijarah. Using fixed effects panel regressions and the Bias-Corrected Least Squares Dummy Variable (LSDVC) method, we reveal a significant and positive impact of halal awareness on total Islamic financing, particularly through Murabaha and Ijarah contracts, which are operationally simpler and more consumer-oriented. Meanwhile, the effect on participatory contracts like Mudarabah and Musharakah is weak, highlighting structural and informational constraints. The results validate the demand-following hypothesis and offer policy insights into the role of digital behavioural signals in shaping Islamic finance strategies. This study contributes to the emerging literature at the intersection of Islamic finance, financial technology, and behavioural economics.

candidates.title: PaECTER: Patent-level representation learning using citation-informed transformers
candidates.introExcerpt: Domain-specific language models have become increasingly critical in the social sciences and technological domains, enabling the transformation of text into valuable data and offering scalable ways to learn semantic similarity across large document collections. In the context of patents, social scientists have shown particular interest in measuring patent similarity to analyze knowledge flows, estimate patent value, and study technological frontiers. For patent examiners, the ability to retrieve relevant prior art precisely and efficiently is essential for timely assessments of the patentability of claimed inventions under patent law and ensuring the quality of patent examinations. Missing any relevant prior patents during prior art searches would risk granting suboptimal patents, which can result in opposition or litigation, increase the burden of rework for the patent office, and undermine the objectives of the patent system. However, existing state-of-the-art tools for document similarity learning are often specifically tailored to scientific English, which structurally and lexically differs from patent language. The PaECTER model (Patent Embeddings using Citation-informed TransformERs) addresses this gap by encoding patents into numerical representations to enable the identification of semantically similar patents. The introduction of Bi-Directional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) [ 1 ] marked a significant advancement for researchers working with text. These models, trained on large textual corpora, produce fixed-size dense vector representations (embeddings) of input text. BERT and its derivatives rely on a predefined vocabulary of tokens, which are either words or sub-words. Out-of-vocabulary tokens are either discarded or broken into smaller, recognizable subwords. This approach can result in incomplete linguistic coverage, particularly in domains with specialized language, motivating the development of domain-specific BERT derivatives. Researchers have responded by developing BERT models tailored to specific domains and corpora. Among them, BERT for Patents [ 2 ] and SciBERT [ 3 ] are pre-trained language models optimized for patent texts and scientific language, respectively. Vocabulary selection plays a crucial role in determining the effectiveness of these models for domain-specific tasks. Our analysis highlights this by showing that only approximately 50% of the vocabulary used in SciBERT overlaps with that of BERT for Patents — underscoring the need for specialized models in patent-related research. However, these models face a limitation when it comes to measuring text similarity. Their training objectives — predicting masked tokens and the next sentence — are not inherently designed for identifying similar documents. To address this limitation, it is necessary to define an appropriate similarity signal and adopt a similarity-focused training objective. Contrastive learning is a machine learning approach well-suited for this purpose. It trains models to identify patterns by emphasizing the recognition of similarities and differences between data points. A key component of this method is the triplet loss function, which relies on specially crafted training data containing explicit signals for similarity and dissimilarity. SPECTER [ 4 ] and SPECTER2 [ 5 ] exemplify the application of this approach. Both models build on SciBERT’s ability to represent scientific language and utilize training datasets composed of triplets. Each triplet includes a query, a related document (e.g., a citation), and an unrelated one (e.g., a non-citation). The original SPECTER model was trained on 684,000 triplets derived from 146,000 query documents, while the more advanced SPECTER2 was trained on over 6 million triplets. By encoding the titles and abstracts of scientific publications, both models have demonstrated superior performance on various downstream tasks in the scientific domain, including topic classification, citation prediction, and recommendation. SEARCHFORMER [ 6 ] applies a similar approach in the patent domain. However, it is designed specifically for comparing patent claims, making it unsuitable for tasks focused on patent titles and abstracts. Additionally, the model is not publicly available. We strive to fill a gap in the literature by providing a model that combines domain-specific vocabulary, citation-induced similarity training, and public availability. To this end, we adopt the contrastive learning technique akin to the SPECTER/SPECTER2 models. Our model is built on “BERT for Patents”, with the training objective to distinguish cited from non-cited patents based on semantic similarity to a focal patent. candidates.conclusionExcerpt: The PaECTER model provides a valuable resource for researchers and practitioners analyzing patent text. It is freely available on HuggingFace and fast to deploy. PaECTER’s main task is that of a citation recommender, i.e., it excels at retrieving related patent literature for instance during the examination process. Though PaECTER can in principle be used for a variety of tasks (semantic distance, classification/clustering, etc.), we recommend users to benchmark several models on these tasks.
candidates.limitationsExcerpt: The PaECTER model has several limitations that are important to consider: Token length constraints. The underlying BERT architecture processes sequences of up to 512 tokens. As a result, PaECTER was trained on patent titles and abstracts, rather than full descriptions or claims, which are central to defining a patent’s legal scope. While the model captures general semantic aspects of patents, it may be less effective at representing their fine-grained technical details. Language scope. The model was trained exclusively on English-language patent texts. It is therefore not directly applicable to non-English patents. Users working with non-English texts should apply high-quality machine translation prior to inference. Temporal relevance. Because the training data reflects existing and past technologies, the model may underperform on emerging innovations not yet well-represented in the dataset. In particular, it may struggle to identify or classify technologies requiring new Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC) categories in the future. This is left for future analysis.

candidates.title: Meat, milk, wool and grain: The animal economy of medieval England (CE 400 to 1400)
candidates.introExcerpt: Much has been written about the animal economy of medieval England (CE 450-1500) but interpretation of the zooarchaeological record has been held back by reliance on artificial periodisation. This study reduces that reliance via a novel approach to data synthesis. A substantial zooarchaeological dataset compiled for the 'Feeding Anglo-Saxon England' project was investigated allowing a more detailed understanding of when change took place and in what form. Key patterns include: a continuation of Roman husbandry practices at some sites throughout the fifth century; an increase in wool production from the early seventh century; the use of dedicated draught cattle from the ninth century, peaking in the eleventh and mid-twelfth centuries, after which the demand for milk, beef and increasing use of horses for arable production caused the use of cattle for draught to decline.

candidates.title: Accuracy and fairness of facial recognition technology in real-world, low-quality police images: An experiment
candidates.introExcerpt: Law enforcement agencies increasingly use facial recognition technology (FRT) to identify suspects, locate missing persons, and generate investigative leads [ 1 ]. In a typical 1:n identification workflow, a probe image is searched against a database and the system returns candidate images for human review; recent work suggests that newer algorithms may make this review stage more difficult by returning more visually plausible nonmatches [ 2 ]. Despite increasing deployment, recent reviews conclude that empirical evidence about the operational effectiveness and equity of FRT in policing remains limited [ 1 ]. As law enforcement gains access to increasing quantities of images collected under uncontrolled conditions, understanding how FRT performs on low-quality images becomes increasingly important. Although FRT is increasingly used, and often promoted as highly accurate ([ 3 ]), the accuracy of FRTs has been tested primarily in settings with high-quality images ([ 4 ]) or in-the-wild image datasets, which contain uncontrolled variation but do not isolate the effects of specific image degradations. Algorithms likely work less well in low-quality images such as those often used by law enforcement. But, the promotion of FRTs being so accurate can lead to law enforcement being misled. For example, a media investigation revealed that some law enforcement officers treat FRT outputs as definitive rather than investigative leads, for example, referring to an unverified match as ‘100% match’ ([ 5 ]). However, the Innocence Project reports that there are “at least seven confirmed cases of misidentification due to facial recognition technology, six of which involve Black people who have been wrongfully accused.” ([ 6 ]). But how often are FRTs making errors with degraded images, and how much worse are errors due to blur than to a face that is turned away? Are errors occurring equally across demographic groups? Without proper validation, using FRT in practice risks contributing to wrongful accusations or wrongful convictions, and this could be worse for individuals of certain demographic characteristics. Law enforcement officers and other stakeholders might trust the FRT results more or less than they should. Prior work has evaluated the performance of both facial recognition algorithms and human facial comparison examiners under controlled conditions ([ 7 ]). A growing literature has also examined how image quality influences FRT accuracy [ 8 – 13 ], including the effects of object motion, camera characteristics, illumination, pose, and resolution. NIST has evaluated large numbers of facial recognition algorithms in both 1:1 and 1:n tasks and across demographic groups ([ 4 ]). More recent studies have directly examined the intersection of image degradation, 1:n identification, and demographic disparities. Atzori et al. documented demographic disparities under low-resolution conditions, although their magnitude and relationship to operating thresholds varied across models and datasets [ 14 ], while Pangelinan et al. found that increasing blur and reducing resolution can sharply degrade 1:n identification performance and alter demographic disparities [ 15 ]. More recent work by Pangelinan et al. showed that degrading both probe and gallery images can substantially increase FPIR and demographic disparities, with nonlinear interactions between probe quality, gallery quality, and the matching algorithm [ 16 ]. Differential accuracy of FRT across demographic groups remains a critical concern. Prior studies have documented differences in error rates by race, gender, and age [ 17 – 20 ], and different methods have been proposed for measuring algorithmic fairness [ 21 – 24 ]. Existing work therefore demonstrates that image quality and demographic characteristics can interact in determining FRT performance. However, relatively little work has systematically varied multiple forms of image degradation over a range of severity levels while separately estimating false positive and false negative identification rates under controlled conditions. Courts have begun to require disclosure when a lead was generated using FRT, and it is likely that FRT results will increasingly be introduced in evidentiary contexts. As of early 2025, 15 states had enacted laws regulating FRT use in policing ([ 25 ]), and courts are beginning to require disclosure when FRT is used. As such, courts’ admissibility standards for scientific evidence offer a valuable framework for evaluating the validity of these tools. Legal scholars have raised concerns about transparency, proprietary algorithms, and contextual bias [ 26 – 30 ]. As FRT moves closer to evidentiary use, its validity, reliability, and error rates will require careful empirical evaluation ([ 31 ]). Our approach draws on lessons learned from problems in traditional forensic science disciplines, specifically, their lack of demonstrated reliability (accuracy, repeatability, and reproducibility) ([ 3
candidates.conclusionExcerpt: This study evaluated the effects of image degradation on the accuracy and fairness of facial recognition technology in 1:n identification tasks relevant to criminal investigations. Using synthetic faces, we systematically examined how blur, pose, brightness, contrast, and resolution influence false positive and false negative identification rates across demographic groups. In addition to estimating overall accuracy, we provide conditional error-rate curves showing how performance changes as image degradation increases across multiple image-quality factors and demographic groups. Our results show that some forms of image degradation have substantially larger effects on performance than others. Reduced resolution has the largest effect on FNIR, while resolution, blur, brightness, and contrast also produce substantial changes in FPIR. Changes in blur, brightness, and contrast additionally produce sizeable increases in FNIR, but their effects are considerably smaller than that of reduced resolution. We also observe differential accuracy across demographic groups: FPIR is often higher for Black individuals, particularly Black women, whereas the demographic groups experiencing the highest FNIR vary across degradation conditions. Benchmark evaluations [ 4 ] often report low error rates under controlled, high-quality image conditions, but these estimates may not reflect performance in degraded surveillance imagery commonly encountered in practice. Together, these findings highlight the importance of evaluating FRT systems under realistic operational conditions rather than relying solely on summary benchmark accuracy estimates.

candidates.title: Methods for cost-efficient, whole genome sequencing surveillance for enhanced detection of outbreaks in a hospital setting
candidates.introExcerpt: Outbreaks of healthcare-associated infections (HAI) result in substantial patient morbidity and mortality; mitigation efforts by infection prevention teams have the potential to curb outbreaks and prevent transmission to additional patients. The incorporation of whole genome sequencing (WGS) surveillance of suspected high-risk pathogens often identifies outbreaks that are not detected by traditional infection prevention methods and provides evidence for transmission. Our approach to real-time WGS surveillance, the Enhanced Detection System for Healthcare-Associated Transmission (EDS-HAT), has 1) identified serious outbreaks that were otherwise undetected and 2) shown the potential to be cost saving.
candidates.conclusionExcerpt: Performing EDS-HAT in real-time can be both feasible and time-efficient. Providing such timely information to aid in outbreak detection could identify transmission events sooner and thus could increase patient safety. candidates.title: Home security cameras as a tool for behavior observations and science affordability
candidates.introExcerpt: Accurately quantifying animal behavior is critical for understanding how organisms respond to challenges and opportunities in their environment, which influences the fitness and survival of a species. Human presence can obscure natural behaviors [ 1 , 2 ], and remote cameras bypass the need for physical presence of the researcher and allows for operationalization of behaviors [ 3 ]. Remote camera approaches are used to study behavior at both population [ 4 , 5 ] and individual levels [ 6 , 7 ]. Mammals and birds are the most common fauna monitored with cameras in the wild, but only a small range of prior studies (<2%) have focused on ectotherms, specifically amphibians and reptiles [ 8 – 10 ]. This gap between ectotherms and endotherms can be explained by both technical and logistical difficulties: many camera traps rely on surface body heat signatures (passive infrared, PIR) warmer than the surrounding environment [ 11 ]. Ectotherms do not produce endogenous body heat higher than the surrounding environment, making PIR camera traps unreliable without experimental background modifications for maximizing heat contrast [ 10 , 12 , 13 ], which is difficult in remote areas or when minimal environmental interference is desired. Moreover, countries in the Global South hold much of the world’s ectotherm biodiversity [ 14 ], yet accessibility and affordability of camera traps for local researchers are prohibitive for this research tool [ 15 ]. Indeed, tropical biomes, which are at highest defaunation risk, are disproportionately less monitored with camera traps compared to other environments [ 15 ]. Increasing camera weather resistance correlates with higher prices, and many camera traps rely on cellular networks headquartered in the Global North, which can present difficulties in network-limited landscapes [ 16 ]. An ideal camera system should be affordable, capable of detecting small ectotherm movement, weather-resistant, and operational in the absence of electricity and phone connectivity. Home security cameras, originally designed for the residential market, offer an affordable alternative class of recording device that can be repurposed for research. These cameras frequently use pixel change detection, which compares pixel values between successive video frames, rather than infrared detection, to trigger recordings [ 17 ]. In daylight, home security cameras use natural lighting for pixel comparisons, and at night, use an active IR system converted into a greyscale image used for pixel change. This enables detection of ectotherm movement, whose body temperature does not differ markedly from ambient conditions. Several home security models are weather-resistant, operate offline, and connect to local Wi-Fi networks rather than depending on cellular providers, which is a key advantage in tropical field sites where Global North cellular coverage is poor or absent. Establishing whether such cameras are suitable for ectotherm behavioral research requires two complementary lines of evidence. First, the affordable camera must perform comparably to established commercial systems under controlled conditions, where independently verified behavior is available for direct comparison. Second, the camera must remain functional and produce ecologically valid data under the real-world conditions, including humidity and temperature extremes, offline operation, and free-ranging animals in complex natural backgrounds. Here, we provide a technical comparison of seven camera systems currently available on the United States market, including affordable home security cameras and camera traps commonly used for research. We then present a two-stage evaluation of a representative system (Wyze v3) for ectotherm behavioral research. First, we benchmark the security camera against an established commercial trail camera (GardePro A3S) in a laboratory terrarium to determine (i) how the two systems compare in the number of behavioral events detected, (ii) how the cameras compare in the duration of behavior recorded per event, and (iii) what fraction of events are recorded by one camera and missed by the other (Study 1). We next validated the system in the field during a 1.5-month deployment in a tropical primary rainforest in a rubric with three independent criteria: hardware survival under tropical conditions, the trade-off between motion-detection sensitivity and event capture, and the ecological validity of laboratory-measured behavioral metrics by comparing paternal visit duration in poison frogs between captive and free-ranging individuals (Study 2). We used two poison frog species as study systems to address different aspects of camera-assisted behavioral monitoring: the relatively large dyeing poison frog ( Dendrobates tinctorius ) served as our laboratory benchmarking system because its larger vivaria could accommodate both camera systems simultaneously, allowing direct comparison while monitoring adult behavior. The variable poison fr
candidates.conclusionExcerpt: Our central motivation for this work is affordability and access to necessary scientific tools. Ectotherms constitute more than 99% of species diversity [ 41 , 42 ], and much of that diversity is in the Global South, where research takes place within a context of historical and current colonialism and economic exploitation [ 43 , 44 ] and where differences in science funding limit which questions can be asked [ 45 ]. Affordable remote monitoring is especially critical where ectotherm biodiversity is greatest and yet equipment budgets are most constrained. While the Wyze v3/v4 is currently shipped directly only within the United States and Canada and import costs can substantially increase the final price, we present it primarily as a proof of concept that home security cameras are viable low-cost alternatives to commercial trail cameras. Comparable systems are available through globally distributed retailers. An additional barrier to the broader use of home security cameras in research is language accessibility: the Wyze app interface and setup materials are primarily available in English. To reduce this limitation, we generated Spanish translations of the Wyze v3 app and quick-start guides, available via GitHub and Protocols.io (dx.doi.org/10.17504/protocols.io.dm6gp3p38vzp/v1), to help counteract the disadvantages created by the dominance of English in science [ 46 ]. We encourage researchers in the Global North to participate in efforts that improve the accessibility of scientific knowledge and research tools through collaboration and shared resources. In summary, affordable home security cameras can match or surpass commercial trail cameras for image and video quality, detection methods, field of view, and motion-detection video length while being less expensive. Their application requires careful attention to sensitivity settings, power logistics, and data management, but the two-stage evaluation we present shows that they represent a substantial expansion of what is affordable for ectotherm behavior research, particularly in regions where the world’s ectotherm biodiversity is concentrated.
